full_judgment:
2. Abdul Kader, predecessor of the opposite parties, as plaintiff, instituted other Class suit No. 66 of 1978 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh for declaration of title to the suit property. The suit property belonged to Upendra Chandra Banik, father of petitioners-defendants Nos. 1 and 2, who was in possession through Bharatia Subal Chandra Modak, Upendra contracted to sell the property to the plaintiff for Tk. 1400/- and received Tk. 700/- in the first part of Ashar, 1369 B.S. It was stipulated that plaintiff would take possession from Subal and Upendra would bear costs. Abdul Kader got possession of the property from Subal on payment of Tk. 700/- to him. Thereafter be requested Upendra to execute and register a kabala but he avoided it. After the death of Upendra, Abdul Kader requested defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to execute and register a kabala but the defendants also avoided it. Then the plaintiff filed a Misc. Case being numbered 48 of 1977 before the House Rent Controller, Kishorgonj for depositing house-rent in favour of the defendants on the allegation that he was a Bharatia under the defendants. The deposit was not accepted by the House Rent Controller on the ground that the plaintiff was a trespasser. Thereafter, Abdul Kader filed the present suit claiming title to the suit property by adverse possession. Abdul Kader died during the pendency of the suit and was substituted by his heirs, the present plaintiff’s opposite-parties. 

 3. Defendants 1 and 2 contested the suit, They denied the alleged contract. Their case was that Abdul Kader had entered the suit property in collusion with Bharatia Subal and in the Rent Control Case had sought to deposit the rent admitting the title of the defendants. The possession of Abdul Kader was never adverse. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit and on appeal the learned Additional District Judge upheld and affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge. Being aggrieved the petitioner’s defendants have moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 5. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties submits that admittedly Abdul Kader had been in possession of the suit property since Ashar, 1369 B.S. and for more than 12 years even before the House Rent Control Case, and he had acquired good title by adverse possession even before the House Rent Control Case and his admission of the defendants in the House Rent Control Case could not destroy that title. 

 6. Admittedly, Abdul Kader had entered into possession of the suit property through the instrumentality of the Bharatia Subal Chandra Modak. The possession of Bharatia Subal was not evidently adverse to the owner landlord Upendra. The possession of any person entering into possession through the instrumentality of the Bharatia could not also be adverse to that of the owner unless such person had set up title in himself in denial of the title of the owner-landlord. It appears that in House Rent Control Misc. Case No. 48 of 1977 filed before the House Rent Controller Abdul Kader had stated that he was a Bharatia tenant under the defendants and he has claimed to deposit house rent admitting the title of the defendants. The possession of a person, however long, cannot be adverse to that of a true owner if he admits the title of the owner. In Premendu Bhusan Mondal Vs. Sripati Ranjan Chakravarty, reported in A.I.R. 1976, Calcutta, 55, it was held that the possession of a person in unauthorised possession admitting title for true owner cannot be adverse to that of the owner but should be deemed to be possession on his behalf. It was also held that a squatter or trespasser who does not Set up a claim of right cannot plead adverse possession and no length of mere squatting possession is a good defence in a suit for possession by true Owner. We see, with respects, no reason to take different view. Abdul Kader admitted the title of the defendants in the House Rent Control Case and there is nothing to show that at any time before this, he had denied the title of the defendants or set up title in himself. A case of the defendants in the House Rent Control Case that Abdul Kader was a trespasser is by no means a material to indicate that Abdul Kader had set up title in himself, particularly when he had himself claimed merely Bharatia right. The courts below have concurrently found that the alleged contract was not proved. They have, however, held that admittedly Abdul Kader was in possession for more than twelve years and as such he acquired title by adverse possession. The courts below have allowed them-selves to fall into error in taking a view that the possession of Abdul Kader was adverse and have committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record, which calls for an interference by this court.
